title: What is database partitioning, and what are the types (horizontal/sharding, vertical, range)?
shortTitle: What is database partitioning, and what are the types

s1_definition.profdef: Database partitioning splits one large logical table into smaller physical pieces called partitions, while the application still sees a single table. Horizontal partitioning divides by rows (each partition holds a subset of rows, e.g. by range, list, or hash of a key); when horizontal partitions live on different servers it becomes sharding. Vertical partitioning divides by columns (splitting a wide table into narrower tables). Range partitioning is a horizontal scheme where each partition owns a contiguous range of the partition key, such as one partition per month.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank's single giant transaction ledger is unwieldy. Partitioning splits it into smaller books. Horizontal partitioning puts different rows in different books — January transactions in one book, February in another (that is range). If those books sit in different branch buildings, that is sharding. Vertical partitioning instead splits the columns — the frequently-read account summary in one slim book and the rarely-read extra details in another. To the teller it still feels like one ledger.
s1_definition.oneliner: Partitioning splits one logical table into smaller physical pieces — horizontally by rows (range/list/hash, and sharding when across servers) or vertically by columns.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Database partitioning splits one large logical table into smaller physical pieces called partitions, while the application still sees a single table. Horizontal partitioning divides by rows (each partition holds a subset of rows, e.g. by range, list, or hash of a key); when horizontal partitions live on different servers it becomes sharding. Vertical partitioning divides by columns (splitting a wide table into narrower tables). Range partitioning is a horizontal scheme where each partition owns a contiguous range of the partition key, such as one partition per month.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank's single giant transaction ledger is unwieldy. Partitioning splits it into smaller books. Horizontal partitioning puts different rows in different books — January transactions in one book, February in another (that is range). If those books sit in different branch buildings, that is sharding. Vertical partitioning instead splits the columns — the frequently-read account summary in one slim book and the rarely-read extra details in another. To the teller it still feels like one ledger.

**One line to remember:** Partitioning splits one logical table into smaller physical pieces — horizontally by rows (range/list/hash, and sharding when across servers) or vertically by columns.

sections.s2_technical:
Partitioning exists because very large tables become hard to manage and slow to query, back up, and maintain. Splitting the table into smaller physical pieces keeps each piece small enough to index efficiently, scan quickly when relevant, and maintain independently, while the application keeps using one table name.

Horizontal partitioning divides by rows. Every partition has the same columns but holds a disjoint subset of the rows, chosen by a partition key. There are three common schemes. Range partitioning assigns each partition a contiguous range of the key — for example `txn_date` from January 1 to January 31 in one partition, February in the next. It is ideal for time-series data and for dropping old data cheaply. List partitioning assigns each partition an explicit set of key values — for example one partition per region, NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST. Hash partitioning assigns rows to partitions by a hash of the key modulo the partition count, which spreads data evenly and avoids hot spots when there is no natural range or list.

Sharding is horizontal partitioning taken across multiple servers. Instead of partitions being separate pieces inside one database instance, each shard is a separate database on its own node. This scales writes and storage beyond a single machine, but introduces cross-shard queries and distributed-transaction challenges that single-instance partitioning does not have. So all shards are partitions, but partitions within one instance are not shards.

Vertical partitioning divides by columns rather than rows. A wide table with many columns is split into narrower tables sharing the same primary key, so the hot, frequently-accessed columns sit in one table and the cold, rarely-read columns in another. For an accounts table, the account id, holder name, and balance that every request needs go in the main table, while large or seldom-used fields like a profile blob or KYC documents go in a side table. This keeps the hot table narrow so more rows fit per page and scans are faster. Normalization is a form of vertical partitioning, and so is splitting out a large text or binary column.

In PostgreSQL, horizontal partitioning is declarative: you create a partitioned table `PARTITION BY RANGE (txn_date)` and attach child partitions. The planner performs partition pruning, skipping partitions that cannot match the query's filter. The key architectural point is that partitioning improves manageability and can improve query performance through pruning, but only when queries filter on the partition key; vertical partitioning improves performance by keeping hot rows narrow; and sharding is the version that scales across machines at the cost of distributed complexity.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's single transactions table has grown to billions of rows and is slow to query and impossible to maintain in one piece. This is exactly what horizontal range partitioning solves — split by month.

Problem 2 — The accounts table is wide, with a big KYC-documents column that is rarely read but loaded on every balance check. This is exactly what vertical partitioning solves — move the cold column to a side table.

Problem 3 — Later the bank outgrows one machine entirely. This is exactly where sharding comes in — horizontal partitions on separate servers.

We will create a range-partitioned transactions table by month, a vertically partitioned accounts design separating hot and cold columns, and a service that reads them, demonstrating each partitioning type.

partitioning-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── src/main/java/com/bank/part/
│   ├── PartApplication.java
│   ├── service/
│   │   └── TransactionService.java

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__range_partition.sql — HORIZONTAL (RANGE) partitioning by month
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id     BIGSERIAL,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    txn_date   DATE NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (txn_id, txn_date)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (txn_date);

-- Child partitions: each owns a contiguous date range
CREATE TABLE transactions_2024_01 PARTITION OF transactions
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');
CREATE TABLE transactions_2024_02 PARTITION OF transactions
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01');

-- LIST partition example (by region) and HASH (even spread) for reference:
-- ... PARTITION BY LIST (region);    FOR VALUES IN ('NORTH','SOUTH')
-- ... PARTITION BY HASH (account_id); FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0)
```

```sql
-- V2__vertical_partition.sql — VERTICAL partitioning (split columns)
-- Hot table: columns every request needs
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id  VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);
-- Cold table: rarely-read, large columns kept out of the hot path
CREATE TABLE account_kyc (
    account_id   VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    kyc_document BYTEA,
    notes        TEXT
);

INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('SAV2001','Rajesh Kumar',1000000.00),
                            ('CUR3001','Priya Sharma',250000.00);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/bankdb
    username: bank_app
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/partitioning-demo-1.0.0.jar

# Insert routes to the right monthly partition automatically
# Query on the partition key prunes partitions:
psql bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT amount FROM transactions \
  WHERE txn_date >= '2024-02-01' AND txn_date < '2024-03-01';"   # scans only transactions_2024_02

# Hot balance read touches only the narrow accounts table (not the KYC blob)
psql bankdb -c "SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id='SAV2001';"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a February transaction insert and a February-only query, plus a balance read.

Step 1: Insert. The transaction has `txn_date = 2024-02-15`. PostgreSQL looks at the partition key and routes the row to `transactions_2024_02` automatically. The application just inserts into `transactions` and never names the partition.

Step 2: Monthly query. The service queries `WHERE txn_date >= '2024-02-01' AND txn_date < '2024-03-01'`. Because the filter is on the partition key, the planner performs partition pruning and scans only `transactions_2024_02`, skipping January and every other month entirely.

Step 3: This is the manageability win too — if we later archive February, we drop one partition instead of deleting billions of rows.

Step 4: Balance read. The hot read touches only the narrow `accounts` table. The large KYC document lives in `account_kyc` and is not loaded, so each row is small and the read is fast. This is vertical partitioning in action.

Step 5: If the bank later outgrows one server, these same horizontal partitions move onto separate nodes as shards, and the application's routing layer directs each account to its shard. The partitioning concept scales from one machine to many.

```
2026-10-25 13:52:10 INFO  TransactionService - Recorded 25000 on 2024-02-15 → partition for FEBRUARY
2026-10-25 13:52:11 INFO  TransactionService - Querying 2024-02-01 to 2024-03-01 — partition pruning skips other months
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ Partitioning Types ═══

  HORIZONTAL (by rows) — one logical table, many row-subset partitions
    transactions (logical)
      ├─ RANGE:  transactions_2024_01 [Jan]
      │          transactions_2024_02 [Feb]   ← insert 2024-02-15 lands here
      ├─ LIST:   by region NORTH / SOUTH / ...
      └─ HASH:   hash(account_id) % 4 → p0..p3 (even spread)

  SHARDING = horizontal partitions on SEPARATE SERVERS
      shard0 [accounts A–H] | shard1 [I–P] | shard2 [Q–Z]

  VERTICAL (by columns) — split a wide table
    accounts(account_id, holder_name, balance)   ← hot, narrow, every request
    account_kyc(account_id, kyc_document, notes)  ← cold, large, rarely read

  Query WHERE txn_date in Feb → partition pruning → scans ONLY Feb partition
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Partitioning Design ═══

  ┌─ Decisions ─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Horizontal RANGE by txn_date → time-series + easy archive│
  │ Vertical split accounts/kyc  → keep hot rows narrow      │
  │ (Future) shard horizontal partitions across nodes        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │     TransactionService        │
  │ - jdbc: JdbcTemplate          │
  │ + record(txn)                 │ → routed to monthly partition
  │ + amountsInMonth(from,to)     │ → partition pruning
  │ + balance(id)                 │ → narrow hot table only
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Types summary (banking):
    Horizontal/range : rows by txn_date (Jan, Feb, ...)
    Horizontal/list  : rows by region (NORTH/SOUTH)
    Horizontal/hash  : rows by hash(account_id) % N (even)
    Sharding         : horizontal partitions on separate servers
    Vertical         : columns split hot (balance) vs cold (kyc)

  Contract:
    Pre:  partition key present on every row
    Post: row lands in exactly one partition; queries on key prune
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Database partitioning splits one large logical table into smaller physical pieces called partitions, while the application still sees a single table. It exists because very large tables become slow to query, back up, and maintain, so keeping each piece small makes indexing, scanning, and maintenance manageable.

There are two broad directions. Horizontal partitioning divides by rows: every partition has the same columns but holds a disjoint subset of the rows chosen by a partition key. It comes in three common schemes. Range partitioning gives each partition a contiguous range of the key, such as one partition per month, which is ideal for time-series data and for dropping old data cheaply. List partitioning gives each partition an explicit set of values, such as one partition per region. Hash partitioning assigns rows by a hash of the key, which spreads data evenly when there is no natural range or list. Vertical partitioning instead divides by columns: a wide table is split into narrower tables sharing the same key, so the hot columns every request needs stay in one narrow table and the cold, large columns move to a side table, which keeps the hot rows small and fast.

Sharding is horizontal partitioning taken across multiple servers, where each shard is a separate database on its own node. So all shards are horizontal partitions, but partitions within a single instance are not shards. Sharding scales writes and storage beyond one machine but adds cross-shard query and distributed-transaction complexity that single-instance partitioning avoids.

At the National Bank of India our transactions table grew into the billions, so I range-partitioned it by month, which let the planner prune to a single month's partition for date-filtered queries and let us archive an old month by dropping one partition instead of deleting billions of rows. Separately, the accounts table carried a large KYC-document column that was loaded on every balance check, so I vertically partitioned it, keeping account id, name, and balance in a narrow hot table and moving the KYC blob to a side table, which made balance reads noticeably faster. The one-line summary I give is that partitioning splits one logical table into smaller physical pieces — horizontally by rows using range, list, or hash, becoming sharding across servers, or vertically by columns.
